endorsements.quote: AI performance should be analyzed across Fitzpatrick skin types, age, sex, anatomical site, and lesion type.
Since darker skin types are consistently under-represented in global datasets, it is essential to perform dedicated analyses and, if necessary, retrain models before deployment in India.
For any model update, a bridging validation should be performed to ensure that accuracy, calibration, and safety remain reliable in real-world settings.
Inform patients when AI contributes to assessment; document consent in workflows where AI influences management.
Informed consent should be obtained when AI influences decision-making, and its role should be documented.
In the Indian context, AI should function as an augmentation tool supporting clinician judgment rather than autonomous diagnosis or treatment.
Clinicians must remain vigilant against automation bias and override AI outputs when clinical context differs.
Structured AI literacy training through continuing medical education or certification is recommended [Figure 2].

Patient-facing dermatology apps that provide diagnostic or treatment suggestions fall under SaMD within the medical device rules 2017 and require CDSCO approval, quality management documentation, and post-market surveillance.
Provide mechanisms for access, correction, and deletion of personal data, and maintain vendor oversight for any third-party processing.
Implement privacy-by-design principles, including data minimization, role-based access control, encryption during data transmission and data storage, audit logs, and secure key management.
Publish model cards that describe scope, training data envelope, known failure modes, and unsupported scenarios (e.g., "not validated in children or acral images").

Pre-deployment bias assessments and ongoing disparity monitoring are essential, with corrective actions (data enrichment, recalibration, subgroup-specific thresholds) and transparent reporting to clinicians.
AI tools should be evaluated in prospective, multi-center studies that reflect real-world clinical practice.
Predictive values should be contextualized to real-world prevalence, and decision-curve analysis should be included to demonstrate clinical utility.
Capture structured metadata (age, sex, site, Fitzpatrick type, device model) to enable bias audits.
Predefined change-control plans and clear triggers for regulatory notification help maintain transparency and compliance.
Shared-liability models, clear instructions for use, and product-liability insurance are recommended.
Policies should mandate explicit patient notification when AI is used, publish model cards, and require encryption, audit logs, and breach-response protocols.

Ensure de-identification of patient data by obscuring identifiable facial features, eyes, or tattoos when these are not clinically essential, and by removing Exchangeable Image File Format/Global Positioning System (EXIF/GPS) metadata from image files.

unlisted_practices: Conduct continuous post-market surveillance of deployed dermatology AI to monitor safety, equity, and performance drift, including public reporting of serious adverse events.
Establish regulatory sandboxes and national dermatology AI registries to track clinical performance, safety events, equity measures, and drift.
Obtain explicit, revocable consent with an opt-out option when patient data are used for continuous learning.
Give preference to AI models that provide explainability through confidence scores, uncertainty flags, rationales, and clearly stated limitations.
Educate patients to treat AI outputs as preliminary guidance, seek professional consultation, and avoid uploading dermatological images to unregulated platforms.
Provide rapid patch and rollback capability and temporarily suspend AI tools with material defects until remediation.
Report sensitivity, specificity, AUC, calibration, confidence intervals, and workflow impact measures in AI performance studies, following standard reporting frameworks.
Evaluate AI tools for cost-effectiveness, subsidize them for primary-care settings, and adapt them for multilingual use to promote equitable access.
Clinical trials of AI should measure meaningful patient outcomes such as faster diagnosis or improved disease control.
Power validation studies to estimate sensitivity and specificity with +/-3-5% precision and perform external validation on previously unseen sites.
Choose safety-first, sensitivity-maximizing thresholds with clear escalation prompts for high-risk indications such as malignancy triage.

screen.reason: This is a position statement and policy framework by the IADVL Academy providing recommendations and guidance on AI adoption in Indian dermatology.
